actions.name: Review audiologic evaluation report from last week
actions.result: Pure tone audiometry: Right ear mild sloping to moderate high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss (20 dB HL at 500 Hz to 50 dB HL at 4000-8000 Hz). Left ear moderate to severe sensorineural hearing loss (40 dB HL at 500 Hz sloping to 75 dB HL at 4000 Hz). Interaural asymmetry exceeds 20 dB at 1000, 2000, 3000, and 4000 Hz. Word recognition scores: 92% right ear, 64% left ear (poorer than predicted by pure-tone average). Tympanometry: Type A bilaterally (normal middle ear pressure and compliance).

actions.name: Calculate pure tone average and compare interaural asymmetry
actions.result: PTA (500/1000/2000 Hz): Right 25 dB HL, Left 47 dB HL. Asymmetry of 20 dB confirmed at multiple frequencies, meeting criteria for asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss.

actions.name: Compare word recognition score to pure-tone average (poorer-than-expected finding)
actions.result: Left ear WRS (64%) is lower than predicted from the left PTA, a retrocochlear 'red flag' pattern of disproportionately poor word understanding relative to the degree of hearing loss.

actions.name: Administer tinnitus history questions (onset, laterality, pulsatile quality, associated symptoms)
actions.result: Patient reports constant, non-pulsatile ringing in the left ear only, gradually worsening since onset, with no right-sided tinnitus. Further questioning clarifies the ringing began roughly a year ago, after she had already noticed some hearing difficulty, though she cannot pinpoint the exact timeline.

actions.name: Screen for vestibular/balance symptoms (dizziness, imbalance, falls)
actions.result: Patient reports occasional brief unsteadiness when turning her head quickly; denies vertigo spells, denies falls, denies true room-spinning sensations.

actions.name: Camera inspection of outer ears and visible ear canal with patient-held flashlight/otoscope
actions.result: Bilateral pinnae and visible canal entrance appear normal; no visible cerumen occlusion, discharge, or structural abnormality on camera.

actions.name: Administer self-report hearing handicap/communication function questionnaire (e.g., HHIE-S)
actions.result: Score consistent with moderate self-perceived hearing handicap; patient endorses difficulty following conversation in groups and has withdrawn from a social activity (bridge club) due to communication difficulty.

actions.name: Review noise exposure and occupational history
actions.result: No history of significant occupational, recreational, or military noise exposure reported.

actions.name: Review past otologic/surgical history for ear disease, trauma, or ear surgery
actions.result: No history of ear infections, ear surgery, head trauma, or ototoxic medication use reported.

actions.name: Determine whether findings meet criteria for urgent medical/ENT referral prior to amplification
actions.result: Asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss (>15 dB difference, multiple frequencies) with unilateral tinnitus and word recognition poorer than predicted meets criteria for referral to otolaryngology/neurotology for evaluation, including consideration of MRI of the internal auditory canals to rule out retrocochlear pathology (e.g., vestibular schwannoma) before finalizing an amplification plan.

actions.name: Review current medication list for ototoxic agents
actions.result: Medication list reviewed; no ototoxic medications (e.g., aminoglycosides, high-dose loop diuretics, platinum chemotherapy) currently prescribed.

artifacts.title: Audiologic Evaluation Report
artifacts.author: Audiology Associates of Savannah
artifacts.body:
REASON FOR REFERRAL: Patient-reported difficulty hearing, urged by spouse to be evaluated.

HISTORY: 68-year-old female reports gradual difficulty understanding conversation, particularly in groups or background noise. Reports constant tinnitus, left ear, x1 year. No reported noise exposure. No vertigo reported at time of testing.

OTOSCOPY: Bilateral ear canals clear, tympanic membranes grossly normal.

TYMPANOMETRY: Type A bilaterally.

PURE TONE AUDIOMETRY:
Right ear: 500 Hz 20 dB HL, 1000 Hz 25 dB HL, 2000 Hz 30 dB HL, 3000 Hz 40 dB HL, 4000 Hz 50 dB HL, 8000 Hz 50 dB HL.
Left ear: 500 Hz 40 dB HL, 1000 Hz 45 dB HL, 2000 Hz 55 dB HL, 3000 Hz 65 dB HL, 4000 Hz 75 dB HL, 8000 Hz 70 dB HL.

SPEECH AUDIOMETRY: Speech Reception Threshold Right 25 dB HL, Left 50 dB HL. Word Recognition Score (NU-6, 50 dB above SRT): Right 92%, Left 64%.

IMPRESSION: Bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, asymmetric, worse left, with word recognition score poorer than predicted for degree of loss in the left ear. Unilateral tinnitus. Recommend medical/ENT referral prior to amplification given asymmetry and WRS findings.

cells: 84-96% (expected for moderate-severe loss) - SCORE LOWER THAN EXPECTED

profile.encounterType: Hearing evaluation results counseling (follow-up to diagnostic audiogram)

facts.chart: Patient presents for review of audiogram results performed one week ago at husband's urging; reports difficulty following conversations, especially in groups.
facts.says: My husband made me go get my hearing tested. I guess I'm here to find out what it means. I don't really think it's as bad as he says, but everybody seems to mumble lately.

facts.chart: Reports gradual onset of difficulty understanding speech, worse in groups or background noise, over past 1-2 years.
facts.says: It's not sudden or anything. It's crept up slow. I notice it most at restaurants or when my grandkids are all talking at once.

facts.chart: Constant, non-pulsatile ringing in left ear only, onset approximately 1 year ago, gradually worsening, no associated right-sided tinnitus.
facts.says: There's this ringing, like a kettle, in my left ear. It's been there about a year now, and it never stops, not even at night.

facts.chart: Occasional brief unsteadiness with quick head turns; denies true vertigo, denies falls.
facts.says: Well, now that you mention it, sometimes if I spin around too fast to answer the phone I feel a little off, just for a second. I didn't think it was worth mentioning.

facts.chart: Denies otalgia, otorrhea, or recent ear infection.
facts.says: No pain, no drainage, nothing like that.

facts.chart: Denies headache, facial numbness, or facial weakness.
facts.says: No headaches, my face feels fine, nothing numb or droopy.

facts.chart: Has stopped attending weekly bridge club due to difficulty following group conversation; feels embarrassed asking people to repeat themselves.
facts.says: I quit my bridge club a few months back. I kept asking 'what?' so much I just felt foolish, so I stopped going.

facts.chart: Expresses strong reluctance toward hearing aids, associating them with aging and loss of independence.
facts.says: I am not wearing one of those big beige things in my ear. Those are for old people. I'm not there yet.

facts.topic: belief about cause of hearing trouble
facts.chart: Attributes hearing difficulty to others' speech habits rather than her own hearing.
facts.says: Honestly, I think people just don't talk clearly anymore. Everybody mumbles. My husband especially.

facts.chart: Denies significant occupational, recreational, or military noise exposure.
facts.says: I was a court stenographer my whole career, sitting quiet in a courtroom. Never worked around loud machinery or anything like that.

facts.topic: ear infections or ear surgery history
facts.chart: Denies history of chronic ear infections, ear surgery, or significant head trauma.
facts.says: No, never had ear surgery, no bad ear infections that I remember, no head injuries.

facts.chart: Denies use of ototoxic medications such as aminoglycoside antibiotics, high-dose loop diuretics, or chemotherapy agents.
facts.says: I just take my blood pressure pill, my cholesterol pill, and a calcium vitamin. Nothing fancy.

facts.chart: Mother had gradual age-related hearing loss in her 70s-80s; no known family history of sudden, asymmetric hearing loss or acoustic neuroma.
facts.says: My mother went deaf in her old age too, but that was just regular old-age hearing loss as far as I know.

facts.chart: Reports subjective sense that left ear is worse than right, though she had attributed overall difficulty mainly to others' speech clarity.
facts.says: Now that I think on it, I probably do hear worse out of my left ear. I favor my right side on the phone without even realizing it.

facts.chart: Denies recent upper respiratory infection, ear fullness, or sudden pressure change preceding symptoms.
facts.says: No colds or anything like that recently. No stuffy ears.

facts.chart: Attending primarily to satisfy spouse's concern rather than from personal conviction of need for treatment.
facts.says: Honestly I'm half here just to get my husband off my back. He's been after me for months.

facts.chart: Reports relying on lip-reading and asking others to repeat themselves, particularly in group settings.
facts.says: I watch people's mouths move, that helps some. And I just ask 'say that again' a lot, which gets old for everybody.

facts.chart: Expresses underlying worry that results may indicate something serious, masked by defensive humor.
facts.says: So is this going to be bad news? Don't sugarcoat it, but also don't scare me half to death either.

facts.chart: Denies sensation of aural fullness or pressure in either ear.
facts.says: No, my ears don't feel full or plugged up, just the ringing on the left.

facts.chart: Retired court stenographer; retired approximately 5 years ago.
facts.says: I retired from court reporting about five years back. Thirty years of taking down every word people said, and now I can't hear half of them.

facts.chart: Reports greatest difficulty in group settings, restaurants, and on the telephone, less difficulty in one-on-one quiet conversation.
facts.says: One-on-one in a quiet room, I do okay. It's groups and restaurants and the phone where I really struggle.

facts.chart: Reports husband also has some hearing difficulty of his own, which she feels contributes to the sense that he mumbles.
facts.says: Honestly my husband mumbles too, he never did speak up clearly, so maybe it's not all me.

facts.chart: Reports mild difficulty with fine print, uses reading glasses; no other visual complaints.
facts.says: I need my reading glasses for the newspaper now, but my eyes are otherwise fine.

facts.topic: follow up with prior doctor about ear symptoms
facts.chart: Did not mention tinnitus or hearing changes to primary care physician at visit 6 months ago.
facts.says: I don't think I said anything to Dr. Nguyen about the ringing. It didn't seem like a big deal at the time, and the visit was really about my blood pressure.

facts.chart: Expresses hesitation about seeing another specialist, concerned about cost and time given she feels the hearing test was already the hard part.
facts.says: Another doctor? I just got through with this test. Do I really have to go see someone else too? That seems like a lot.

facts.topic: timeline of tinnitus versus hearing loss onset
facts.chart: Reports tinnitus onset (about 1 year ago) came after she had already noticed some hearing difficulty, though she cannot pinpoint exact timeline precisely.
facts.says: The ringing started maybe a year ago. I think I was already having some trouble hearing before that, but it's hard to say exactly when.

facts.chart: Reports increased frustration and some tension at home related to communication difficulty, particularly with television volume and phone calls.
facts.says: My husband gets a little short with me about the TV being too loud. We've got some bickering over that, I'll admit.

facts.chart: Associates accepting hearing aids with an unwelcome marker of old age and loss of sharpness she prided herself on in her career.
facts.says: I spent my whole career being the sharpest person in the room, catching every word. Admitting I can't hear right feels like giving up something I was proud of.

facts.chart: Denies nausea, vomiting, or other autonomic symptoms accompanying the brief unsteadiness.
facts.says: No, I don't get sick to my stomach or anything with that dizzy feeling, it's really brief.

facts.topic: what she wants from this visit
facts.chart: States goal of understanding test results clearly and wanting practical options without being pressured into hearing aids immediately.
facts.says: I just want to know plainly what the test showed, and I don't want to feel pushed into buying something today.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient believes she never mentioned the tinnitus or hearing changes to her primary care doctor because it didn't seem important at the time.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Prior primary care note from 6 months ago documents no complaints of dizziness, hearing changes, or tinnitus, and states the patient did not raise any ear-related concerns at that visit.
mismatches.teachingPoint: The chart confirms the patient's recollection, but it also reveals a missed opportunity for earlier identification of asymmetric loss and tinnitus; this reinforces the importance of routine hearing/tinnitus screening questions in primary care and timely referral once red flags are identified.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient reports she does okay with one-on-one conversation in a quiet room and that her main difficulty is only in groups, restaurants, and on the phone.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Word recognition testing shows the left ear scores only 64% even in the controlled, quiet test-booth setting at a comfortable loud presentation level, which is lower than expected for the degree of loss - meaning her left-ear word understanding is reduced even without background noise.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients often underestimate difficulty in quiet one-on-one settings because they compensate by favoring the better ear or using visual cues; objective word recognition testing in a controlled setting can reveal a real deficit that self-report alone may miss, which is especially important here given the retrocochlear red flag pattern.

objectives.text: Identify asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss and recognize the audiometric red-flag criteria (interaural asymmetry, poorer-than-expected word recognition) that warrant medical referral rather than proceeding directly to amplification.
Elicit and characterize unilateral tinnitus and associated vestibular symptoms through directed history-taking, recognizing their relevance as red flags when paired with asymmetric hearing loss.

Formulate an appropriate referral recommendation (ENT/neurotology evaluation, consideration of MRI internal auditory canals) consistent with audiology scope of practice, rather than diagnosing the underlying etiology directly.
Assess the psychosocial and functional impact of hearing loss, including social withdrawal and stigma around hearing aids, to inform patient-centered counseling.
Identify and sensitively explore a patient-versus-chart mismatch regarding prior disclosure of symptoms and self-reported versus tested communication difficulty.
Counsel the patient on next steps that respect her stated goals (clear explanation, no pressure to purchase hearing aids immediately) while clearly conveying the medical urgency of the referral.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Asymmetric bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (worse left) with unilateral tinnitus and word recognition score poorer than predicted for degree of loss in the left ear - an audiologic red-flag pattern requiring medical referral to rule out retrocochlear pathology before finalizing an amplification plan.
differential: Bilateral age-related (presbycusis) sensorineural hearing loss with coincidental asymmetry
Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) or other retrocochlear/cerebellopontine angle lesion
Meniere's disease or other unilateral inner ear disorder
Sudden or progressive idiopathic unilateral sensorineural hearing loss of other etiology
keyFindings: Interaural asymmetry exceeding 20 dB at multiple frequencies (right PTA 25 dB HL vs left PTA 47 dB HL)
Left ear word recognition score (64%) poorer than predicted for degree of pure-tone loss
Constant unilateral (left-sided) non-pulsatile tinnitus of 1 year duration
Occasional brief unsteadiness with quick head turns, though no frank vertigo or falls
Normal tympanometry bilaterally, ruling out conductive/middle ear contribution
Significant self-reported social and functional handicap (HHIE-S moderate range), including withdrawal from bridge club
plan: Refer to otolaryngology/neurotology for medical evaluation of asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss with unilateral tinnitus

Communicate to referring/receiving physician the specific audiometric red flags (asymmetry magnitude, WRS discrepancy) to support consideration of MRI of the internal auditory canals to evaluate for retrocochlear pathology (e.g., vestibular schwannoma)
Do not finalize bilateral hearing aid fitting until medical evaluation is complete, though discussion of amplification options and realistic expectations can begin in parallel with patient consent

Counsel patient using patient-centered, destigmatizing language regarding hearing aids, directly addressing her 'hearing aids are for old people' belief and connecting amplification benefit to her stated goal of returning to valued activities such as bridge club
Address psychosocial impact: validate frustration and the loss of identity tied to her prior career of catching every word; offer continued support regardless of her decision pace

Educate on the difference between what quiet one-on-one testing shows (reduced left-ear word understanding even without noise) and her self-perception of only struggling in groups/noise, to build insight without being pressured into decisions
Document findings clearly in the audiologic evaluation report and ensure follow-up loop closure once referral results are available
redFlags: Asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss greater than 15 dB difference at multiple frequencies
Word recognition score significantly poorer than predicted for the degree of hearing loss in one ear
New or unexplained unsteadiness/imbalance in the context of asymmetric hearing loss
educationPoints: Asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss combined with unilateral tinnitus and/or poorer-than-expected word recognition is a recognized audiologic red-flag pattern warranting referral to rule out retrocochlear pathology such as vestibular schwannoma, even in the absence of dramatic vertigo.

Audiologists play a critical gatekeeping role: identifying these patterns and making a timely, clearly-communicated referral is within scope, while diagnosing the underlying cause (e.g., confirming or excluding acoustic neuroma) is outside scope and belongs to the medical referral partner.

Stigma around hearing aids can be a major barrier to care; patient-centered counseling that connects amplification to the patient's own valued activities and identity (rather than generic 'you need hearing aids') improves acceptance and follow-through.

Self-reported difficulty (worse in noise, fine one-on-one) can underestimate true impairment; objective word recognition testing in quiet, controlled conditions can reveal deficits the patient has not recognized or has compensated for using visual or contextual cues.

Missed opportunities for earlier detection can occur when patients do not volunteer otologic symptoms to non-specialist providers during visits focused on other chronic conditions, underscoring value of routine screening questions.

patient.name: Dorothy Greenwood
patient.appearance: A trim, silver-haired woman sits upright at a kitchen table with good overhead lighting, wearing a crisp cardigan and reading glasses pushed up on her head. Her posture is alert and her expression is often wry or slightly guarded, with sharp, attentive eyes that track the screen closely. A faint ringing-related tension shows in brief pauses when she turns her head toward sounds off-camera.

persona.personality: Sharp-witted, proud, and a little defensive; values precision and self-sufficiency from decades of exacting courtroom work.
persona.communicationStyle: Direct and quick with dry humor, deflects vulnerability with jokes or mild sarcasm, but softens when she feels genuinely heard rather than lectured.
persona.emotionalState: Outwardly composed and faintly annoyed at having to be here, with an undercurrent of worry she tries to mask with wit.
persona.background: Worked thirty years as an official court stenographer in Savannah, prided herself on catching every word spoken in the courtroom; retired five years ago. Married to her husband Walter for 42 years; two adult children live out of state. Enjoys crossword puzzles, gardening, and until recently a weekly bridge club with longtime friends.
speechExamples: I didn't come here for a lecture, I came here for answers.
Honestly, I think people just mumble more than they used to.
I spent my career catching every word in that courtroom - now I'm the one who can't follow along.
Don't sugarcoat it, but don't scare me to death either.
Another doctor? Lord, when does this end.
concerns: Worried the test results mean something is seriously wrong, though she downplays this openly
Does not want to be pressured into buying hearing aids before she is ready
Concerned about cost and time involved in seeing yet another specialist
Fears losing her sense of sharpness and independence that defined her career identity

scenario.studentBrief: You are an audiology student conducting a telehealth follow-up visit with Dorothy Greenwood, a 68-year-old woman who had a diagnostic audiogram one week ago at her husband's urging. Your task is to review her audiologic test results with her, take a focused history, assess the functional and psychosocial impact of her hearing loss, and determine appropriate next steps within your scope of practice as an audiology student.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Follow-up visit to review audiogram results and discuss difficulty understanding conversation, particularly in groups.
scenario.openingLine: My husband made me come get this hearing thing checked out. I guess you're going to tell me what the test showed - though I'll warn you, I still think most people just mumble.
tasks: Review and explain the audiogram and word recognition results in plain language appropriate to her health literacy
Take a focused history of the presenting concern, including functional impact of hearing loss and attitudes toward management options
Assess for any additional relevant symptoms
Determine appropriate next steps within your scope of practice
Counsel the patient on your recommendations and agree on a plan

profile.setting: Telehealth video visit; patient at home at her kitchen table in Savannah, Georgia
profile.summary: Dorothy Greenwood, a 68-year-old retired court stenographer, presents for telehealth counseling on a diagnostic audiogram showing asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss (worse left) with unilateral tinnitus and left-ear word recognition poorer than predicted for the degree of loss - a classic audiologic red-flag pattern requiring medical referral to rule out retrocochlear pathology before amplification. The case teaches learners to recognize referral criteria within audiology scope, elicit sensitive psychosocial barriers to hearing aid acceptance, and navigate a patient who minimizes her symptoms and resists the idea of hearing aids.
profile.title: Asymmetric Sensorineural Hearing Loss with Unilateral Tinnitus: Results Counseling and Referral Decision
